imageCaption: Luisana's journal lies open on the kitchen table, surrounded by coffee rings and pressed flowers, as she frowns at a question she's written but doesn't know how to answer.
text:
Aaliyah found her mother in the kitchen at 11:47 PM, which was the kind of time that suggested either insomnia or a thought so important it had woken her up.

It was the journal. It was always the journal.

Luisana was sitting at the coral table—the one that had known it was coral from the beginning and had maintained that conviction even when the house was still deciding what it wanted to be—with her notebook open and her handwriting scattered across the page like she'd been writing in different directions simultaneously. The pressed morpho butterfly from the doorstep was sitting on top of the journal, not held in place by anything, just resting there like it had weight.

"Can't sleep?" Aaliyah asked, pulling out the chair that was becoming increasingly hers, the one next to Sully's favorite spot under the table.

"Can't stop," Luisana said. She didn't look up from the page. "There's a difference. Can't sleep means I'm anxious. Can't stop means I'm trying to understand something and the understanding won't arrive unless I keep asking."

She finally looked up. Her eyes had that red-rimmed clarity that came from thinking very hard about very real things for several hours without stopping.

"What do you write in a journal when you're supposed to be staying somewhere?" Luisana asked. "When the story you're documenting isn't *going* anymore, it's *building*?"

Aaliyah pulled the chair closer. The question hung in the kitchen air between them—the kind of question that parents asked children when they were actually looking for the answer, not pretending they already had it.

"You write what you're noticing," Aaliyah said slowly. "You write what scares you about it. You write what you're hoping for. You write what's different between when you were running and when you stopped."

She paused. "That's what you've always done. You don't journal the facts. You journal the feelings about the facts. You journal the questions that won't be answered until they're written down and then stared at for a while."

Luisana smiled faintly. "This is why I worry about you. You understand things too clearly. You're going to understand someone completely one day and realize you can't be surprised by them anymore, and I don't think that's going to make you happy."

"Story problem," Aaliyah said. "I'm fine with story problems."

Her mother set down her pen and pushed the journal slightly toward the center of the table, which was her way of inviting Aaliyah into whatever was happening inside her brain.

The page was mostly questions. Not observations—Luisana had pages and pages of observations. These were different. These were the kind of questions that needed answers that weren't in any guidebook.

*What does it mean to choose a place when you've spent your whole life choosing movement?*

*How do I know if I'm staying because I want to or because I'm tired?*

*What does Anthony see in Curaçao that I keep running toward in real estate listings at midnight?*

*When does a family stop being defined by running toward and start being defined by standing still?*

*What do I do with all this motion when I finally have somewhere to put it down?*

"That's it," Luisana said. "That's the thing I can't answer. I spent seventy-four days documenting a family healing a timeline by being spontaneous and chaotic and real with each other. I did what I always do—I observed, I asked questions, I tried to understand how things worked. And now I'm supposed to put that same energy into building a life here, and I don't know how to build something. I know how to watch things. I know how to investigate. I know how to notice when something matters."

"You're watching this matter," Aaliyah said, pointing at the journal. "You're investigating what staying means. You're building the story of *how* we stay, not just *that* we stay. That's different from running. That's not a lower intensity. It's just a slower burn."

Luisana picked up the butterfly. It sat in her palm with the kind of fragility that made you very aware of how careful you had to be with beautiful things.

"Abuela Ida taught your father that the best things in life are unplanned," she said quietly. "And he lived that. He lived that so completely that he accidentally healed the world. But your father got his definition of spontaneity from his grandmother. He had roots before he learned to run. He was grounded in something—in Abuela Ida's kitchen, in her philosophy, in her certainty. When he ran, he was running *from* something solid. When he stopped, he was running *back* to something."

She set the butterfly down carefully. It didn't move. It had the presence of something that belonged exactly where it was.

"I don't have an Abuela Ida," Luisana continued. "My parents were investigators too. My grandmother was a journalist in Cuba before she died. We were all people who asked questions and moved places. I never had roots. And now I'm supposed to grow them, and I don't know if I'm going to grow them right. If I'm going to grow them the way this neighborhood needs me to. If I'm going to be the kind of person who brings a dish to dominoes and means it."

"You're already that person," Aaliyah said. "You've been that person. You just thought you had to be moving to be that person, so you didn't notice."

She reached over and touched the corner of the journal. "Write that. Write that the person who asks the best questions, who notices what matters, who falls in love with families and cities and coffee shops and men who buy airplane tickets without telling their wives—that person was always someone who belonged to places. You were always staying. You just didn't know you were allowed to."

Luisana's eyes got very shiny. She picked up her pen.

"I'm going to write something that you can't unhear now," she said. "I'm going to write it and it's going to become true because I wrote it down."

"Okay," Aaliyah said. "Write the true thing."

Luisana bent over her journal.

*We are staying. I am staying. This is not a rest stop. This is home. Now I get to figure out what that means.*

She set down the pen and looked at her daughter across the table.

"Saturday," Luisana said softly. "We need to make something that tells the neighborhood who we are."

Aaliyah nodded. She already understood. The dominoes weren't confused anymore. The street was waiting for the family to be confused.

And that was going to be the thing that finally stabilized everything.
